name: Zapata Swamp
blurb: Cuba's great swamp: mangroves, sawgrass and the rare crocodiles that hunt them.

tip.title: Remove the hutias
tip.text: Hutias are prey for the Cuban boa, both crocodiles and scavenging vultures. Set Desmarest's hutia to -100% and watch the top predators lose a main food source.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Warm tropical sun drives plant growth across the open swamp, mangrove fringe and woodland.

nodes.name: Freshwater flooding
nodes.desc: Water covering the low, flat peninsula for much of the year keeps the swamp a wetland and shapes its marsh vegetation.

nodes.name: Brackish coastal water
nodes.desc: Salty water along the southern coast and lagoons supports mangroves, which tolerate salt.

nodes.name: Soil and peat nutrients
nodes.desc: Nutrients held in wetland soil are recycled from dead plants and animals and feed new plant growth.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead sawgrass, mangrove litter and animal remains, returning nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Red mangrove
nodes.desc: Salt-tolerant tree with prop roots; its thickets give nesting and hunting habitat to fish, birds and crocodiles.

nodes.name: Jamaica sawgrass
nodes.desc: Tall sedge of flooded marsh. The endangered Zapata rail nests in it, and dry-season burning of it destroys that habitat.

nodes.name: Scarletbush
nodes.desc: Shrub with nectar-rich flowers and small fruit; GloBI records bats, birds and butterflies feeding on it.

nodes.name: Pigeon berry
nodes.desc: Coastal tree with small fruit; GloBI records Cuban hutia and warblers feeding on it.

nodes.name: Jamaican fruit bat
nodes.desc: Fruit-eating bat that feeds on swamp-edge plants such as scarletbush and spreads seeds as it roams.

nodes.name: Desmarest's hutia
nodes.desc: Large tree-dwelling rodent eating mostly bark, leaves and fruit. Common where mangroves are abundant and a key prey item.

nodes.name: Red-legged thrush
nodes.desc: Thrush that eats fruit and invertebrates, GloBI records it taking scarletbush.

nodes.name: Gray catbird
nodes.desc: Winter visitor that eats fruit and insects in thickets, including scarletbush and West Indian milkberry.

nodes.name: Gulf fritillary
nodes.desc: Butterfly that visits flowers such as scarletbush; prey of dragonflies like the eastern pondhawk.

nodes.name: Knight anole
nodes.desc: Large Cuban tree lizard of forest and mangrove that eats insects, snails and fruit, and sometimes small vertebrates.

nodes.name: Cuban tree frog
nodes.desc: Big, voracious frog that eats nearly anything it can swallow; knight anoles and various snakes prey on it.

nodes.name: Eastern pondhawk
nodes.desc: Predatory dragonfly of ponds and marshes that catches other insects, including butterflies like the Gulf fritillary.

nodes.name: American kestrel
nodes.desc: Small falcon that GloBI records eating tree frogs, lizards and small songbirds such as the gray catbird.

nodes.name: Turkey vulture
nodes.desc: Scavenger that finds carrion by smell and eats almost only dead animals, helping remove carcasses from the swamp.

nodes.name: Cuban boa
nodes.desc: Large constrictor; top land predator in Cuba, eating mostly mammals and birds, including hutias and fruit bats.

nodes.name: Cuban crocodile
nodes.desc: Endemic crocodile whose only wild population is in Zapata Swamp. Adults eat small mammals, fish and turtles.

nodes.name: American crocodile
nodes.desc: Coastal and brackish-water crocodile with a broad diet of fish, birds, mammals, frogs and lizards; hybridizes with Cuban crocodile.
